newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Tribunal won't protest at lifting Serbia sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Tribunal won't protest at lifting Serbia sanctions.

text.p: The new chief prosecutor at the U.N. tribunal for the former Yugoslavia said on Thursday she would not protest against a decision to lift sanctions against Serbia when she met the U.N. Secretary General next week.

"It is not for me to comment on the appropriateness of the lifting of sanctions and I have no intention of raising the issue," Canadian judge Louise Arbour told a news conference two days after taking up her new post in The Hague.
The tribunal has in the past accused Serbia of dragging its feet over the process of delivering indicted suspects.

Late on Tuesday, the U.N. Security Council voted 15-0 to formally end embargoes on trade, travel and transport that had already been suspended in November against the Yugoslav republics of Serbia and Montenegro.

Arbour, who took over from Richard Goldstone of South Africa on Tuesday, reaffirmed that she wanted NATO-led forces to be given a fresh mandate to arrest indicted war criminals in the former Yugoslavia.
"IFOR's presence offers an opportunity which I think it is regrettable has not been fully explored in the past and I believe will be put to better use in the future."
Failure to do, she said, could have serious consequences.
"If the tribunal does not get the assistance...in its efforts to bring indicted war criminals to trial, its perceived failure may exacerbate the tensions it was designed to appease."
She blamed this perceived failure on insufficient co-operation from countries housing fugitive war criminals.
"This matter must be urgently resolved," she said.

The tribunal, set up in 1993 as the first international body for the prosecution of war criminals since the Nuremburg and Tokyo trials after World War Two, has indicted over 70 Serbs, Croats and Moslems. It holds seven suspects in its custody.
